verses.context: The chapter opens with a date and a crisis. Two northern kings march on Jerusalem, and when the news reaches the palace the king and his people shake like trees in a gale. Verse 1 summarizes the outcome in advance (they could not take the city), so the tension of the chapter lies not in whether Jerusalem falls but in whether Ahaz will trust God.
verses.grammar: Verse 1 is almost word for word the same as 2 Kings 16:5, so Isaiah's editors have tied the prophet's story to the royal annals. "Aram was in league with Ephraim" renders nachah Aram al-Efrayim, literally ‘Aram has settled on Ephraim’: the verb nuach, ‘to rest, settle’, pictures Aramean troops camped in Israelite territory, the alliance made visible. The simile in verse 2 uses the same verb twice, vayyana ... kenoa, ‘it shook ... as the shaking of’ the trees. The house of David (beit David) is named as the one who hears the report: the dynasty itself is threatened, a theme that returns in verse 13.
verses.history: The war is the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of about 734 to 732 BC. Ahaz (a short form of Jehoahaz) appears under that fuller name in a list of kings paying tribute in a summary inscription of the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III, alongside kings of Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Ashkelon. The same king's records name Rezin of Damascus as a tribute payer and later as defeated, and report that after Pekah was overthrown Tiglath-pileser set Hoshea on Israel's throne, matching 2 Kings 15:30.

verses.context: God sends Isaiah with his son to meet Ahaz at a precise spot, the end of the conduit of the upper pool. The king is almost certainly inspecting his water supply against a siege. Isaiah meets him at the place of his practical fears with a word about trust.
verses.grammar: The boy's name, Shear-yashuv, means ‘a remnant will return’. The Hebrew order puts ‘remnant’ first, and the phrase can be heard as threat (only a remnant) or as promise (a remnant will come back), both senses Isaiah develops in 10:20-22. "Return" (shuv) is also the ordinary Hebrew word for repenting, so the name may mean a remnant will turn back to God. The child's presence is itself part of the message: Isaiah says in 8:18 that he and his children are signs in Israel.
verses.history: The same place, the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Launderer's Field, is where the Assyrian officer called the Rabshakeh will stand to demand Jerusalem's surrender a generation later (Isaiah 36:2). The echo is deliberate: Ahaz in chapter 7 refuses to trust God at this spot, while his son Hezekiah in chapters 36 and 37 trusts God and the city is spared. The exact location is uncertain; it lay outside the walls, perhaps near the Gihon spring on the city's east side or on the north.

verses.context: Isaiah's first message to Ahaz is to be calm, and then he explains why. The two kings who look like a firestorm are really the smoking ends of two burnt-out sticks. Verses 5 and 6 quote their plan, to break Judah open and install a puppet king, so that verse 7 can overturn it.
verses.grammar: Hishamer vehashqet, "Calm down and be quiet", is a Niphal imperative of shamar, ‘take care, keep yourself’, and a Hiphil imperative of shaqat, ‘be still’. The picture of the two kings is contemptuous: zanvot haudim haashenim, ‘the two tails of these smoking firebrands’, sticks already burned down to stubs. Pekah is never named in the chapter, only called ‘the son of Remaliah’, a way of denying him royal dignity. In verse 6 the verbs are cohortatives, ‘let us go up ... let us tear it apart ... let us break it open’. The puppet's name is vocalized Taveal, which in Hebrew sounds like ‘good for nothing’; many scholars think the original name was Tavel, ‘God is good’, and that the vowels make a pun.

theology.note: Before any command, Isaiah names the fear. The first word of faith in this chapter is not a doctrine but a posture, quietness before a threat that looks larger than it is. Isaiah will state the same principle in 30:15: in quietness and trust is your strength.

verses.context: The Lord's verdict on the plot: it will not stand. The reason is almost dismissive. Aram's head is only Damascus and Damascus's head only Rezin; Ephraim's head is only Samaria and Samaria's only the son of Remaliah. The unspoken conclusion is that Judah's head is the LORD. The oracle ends with the chapter's central line, a challenge to Ahaz to believe.
verses.grammar: Verse 9 closes with one of the most famous wordplays in the Bible: im lo taaminu ki lo teamenu. Both verbs come from aman, ‘to be firm’. The first is a Hiphil, taaminu, ‘you believe’, that is, you rest your weight on something firm; the second is a Niphal, teamenu, ‘you will be made firm, established’. English can only approximate it: ‘If you will not stand firm in faith, you will not stand firm at all’ or ‘no confirm, no firm’. The verbs are plural, addressed to the whole royal house, not Ahaz alone. The word ki before the second clause is unusual; most grammarians take it as emphatic (‘surely’) rather than causal. The "head" (rosh) repeated four times in verses 8 and 9 builds an argument by pattern: every enemy capital and king is named, and the missing line is Judah's.
verses.text: The Septuagint renders the second verb as ‘neither will you understand’ (oude me synete), perhaps reading a different Hebrew verb or interpreting freely. Through the Old Latin that followed the Greek, the line became ‘unless you believe, you will not understand’, which Augustine quoted repeatedly as the charter for faith seeking understanding. Anselm of Canterbury echoes it at the close of the first chapter of his Proslogion (1078). The Hebrew is about stability, not knowledge, but the Greek reading shaped a thousand years of Christian thought about faith and reason.

theology.note: Faith in this verse is not an opinion but a place to stand. The same root gives amen and emunah, faithfulness. Isaiah calls the king to lean his weight on God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16, whose promise that David's house will endure uses the same Niphal verb, neeman), and warns that there is no other footing.

The plans of kings do not determine what happens: "It will not arise; it will not happen." The verse sets out Isaiah's conviction, developed in 14:24-27, that the LORD's purpose stands while human schemes against it fail.

verses.context: God speaks again, now offering Ahaz any sign he wants, from the depths to the heights. Ahaz declines with a pious-sounding refusal: he will not test the LORD. The refusal is the chapter's turning point, since it is not humility but a decision already made to rely on Assyria (2 Kings 16:7-9).
verses.grammar: Heameq sheolah o hagbeah lemaelah uses two Hiphil infinitives absolute, ‘make it deep ... or make it high’: the offer is unlimited. The word read as "Sheol" is ambiguous in the Hebrew consonants: it can be vocalized sheolah, ‘to Sheol’, balancing ‘upwards’, or taken as a lengthened imperative, ‘ask it’. The ancient versions and most modern Bibles read Sheol, the realm of the dead. Ahaz's answer, lo anasseh, uses the Piel of nasah, the verb of Deuteronomy 6:16 (do not put the LORD your God to the test). He quotes the law against the God who gave it: testing God is forbidden when it demands proof in unbelief, not when God himself offers a sign (compare Gideon, Judges 6:36-40, and Hezekiah, Isaiah 38:7-8).

theology.note: Ahaz's sin is unbelief dressed as piety. The chapter shows that refusing God's offered help, while privately trusting another power, can sound like reverence and be the opposite.

verses.context: Isaiah turns from Ahaz to the whole house of David. The refusal has worn out not only human patience but God's. The shift prepares for the sign of verse 14, which is given to the dynasty rather than to Ahaz personally.
verses.grammar: The imperatives and pronouns are now plural (shimu, "Hear"; mikkem, ‘for you all’), addressed to beit David, the royal house. The verb is laah in the Hiphil, ‘to make weary’, used twice: to weary men, and to weary my God. The possessive has shifted: in verse 11 Isaiah said to Ahaz "the LORD your God"; here he says "my God". The prophet no longer calls him Ahaz's God, and the grammar registers the breach.

theology.note: God's promise was made to the house of David (2 Samuel 7), and it is the house of David that Isaiah addresses. The sign that follows is God's answer to the dynasty's unbelief: the covenant will stand, but not through this king's faith.

verses.context: God gives the sign Ahaz refused: a young woman is pregnant, or will be, and will bear a son named Immanuel, ‘God with us’. The next two verses tie the sign to a timetable (before the boy can choose good and reject evil, the two threatening kings will be gone), and the Immanuel name returns in 8:8 and 8:10 and grows into the royal child of 9:6-7 and the shoot of Jesse in 11:1. Few verses have been argued over more.
verses.grammar: Lakhen, "Therefore", in Isaiah usually introduces judgment, and the sign here cuts both ways: deliverance from Rezin and Pekah, and the Assyrian flood of verses 17 to 25. Adonai hu, "the Lord Himself", stresses that God acts where Ahaz would not. The central clause, hinneh haalmah harah veyoledet ben, uses a set formula for announcing a birth: hinneh with an adjective (harah, ‘pregnant’) and a participle (yoledet, ‘bearing’). The same formula appears when the angel speaks to Hagar (Genesis 16:11) and to Manoah's wife (Judges 13:5). Harah is an adjective, not a verb, so it carries no tense: it can mean ‘is pregnant’ or ‘will be pregnant’, and context decides. Almah, with the article, is ‘the young woman’. It occurs seven times in the singular or plural outside musical headings (Genesis 24:43, Exodus 2:8, Psalm 68:25, Proverbs 30:19, Song of Solomon 1:3 and 6:8, and here). It means a girl or young woman of marriageable age; it is never clearly used of a married woman, and in Song 6:8 it names a group distinct from queens and concubines. The word for a virgin in the strict sense is betulah, though even that sometimes needs qualifying (Genesis 24:16). The article may point to a woman known to Isaiah and the court, or it may be generic.
verses.text: The verb veqarat, ‘and she will call’, is a third feminine singular, though the same spelling can be an old second feminine form, ‘and you will call’, as in Genesis 16:11. The great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaa) reads a form that most scholars take as ‘and he will call’ or ‘and one will call’. The Septuagint, translated by Jews in Egypt probably in the second century BC, renders almah with parthenos, usually ‘virgin’, and the verb as kaleseis, ‘you (Ahaz) will call’. Parthenos was not always technical: the Septuagint uses it of Dinah after she had been violated (Genesis 34:3). In the second century AD the Jewish Greek translators Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion all used neanis, ‘young woman’; Irenaeus already objects to Theodotion's and Aquila's rendering (Against Heresies 3.21.1). English Bibles divide the same way: ‘virgin’ in the KJV, NIV, ESV, and BSB; ‘young woman’ in the RSV, NRSV, and the Jewish Publication Society's translation.
verses.history: An Ugaritic poem about the marriage of the moon god Yarikh to the goddess Nikkal, from the thirteenth century BC or earlier, contains a close parallel formula, announcing that a young woman (glmt, the cognate of almah) will bear a son; it shows the phrase was traditional birth-announcement language. Jewish interpreters have identified the mother and child in several ways. Trypho, Justin Martyr's Jewish partner in his Dialogue with Trypho (chapters 43 and 67), refers the verse to Hezekiah; Rashi identifies the young woman with Isaiah's own wife, the mother of the son of 8:3. Christian scholarship divides too. Edward J. Young and J. Alec Motyer, in their commentaries on Isaiah, argue that the verse speaks directly of the Messiah's virginal conception and that no ordinary birth could bear the name and titles of 7:14 to 9:7. Raymond E. Brown, in The Birth of the Messiah (1977), argued that Isaiah meant a child of his own day and that Matthew reads the Greek text in the light of Jesus' conception. Many others hold that a near sign in Ahaz's day and a fuller fulfillment in Christ belong together.

theology.note: The child's name says what the sign is: God with us. Isaiah's first readers heard it as a promise that God would be present to save Judah. The New Testament hears it as a statement of who Jesus is, God come to be with his people in human flesh, and Matthew frames his Gospel with it (Matthew 1:23, 28:20).

The sign is given to the house of David at the moment its king has failed. The child who bears the name Immanuel is tied in the following chapters to the land (8:8) and to the royal son whose government has no end (9:6-7), so the hope for David's line is carried not by Ahaz but by a child God himself provides.

The verse is the classic test case for how prophecy works. Some read it as direct prediction; others as a sign fulfilled first in Isaiah's day and fully in Christ; others as a pattern Matthew recognizes in Jesus, as he does with Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15. All three readings agree that the promise of God's presence with David's house outruns any child born in Ahaz's reign.

nt.note: Matthew quotes the Septuagint nearly word for word: the parthenos will conceive (literally ‘have in the womb’, en gastri hexei) and bear a son. He makes two changes. Where the Greek has ‘you will call’ (kaleseis), Matthew has ‘they will call’ (kalesousin), so the name becomes the confession of the people who receive the child; and he adds the translation, ‘God with us’. The quotation is the first of Matthew's formula citations (‘this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet’), placed right after the angel tells Joseph that the child is conceived from the Holy Spirit (1:20). Matthew's point is not that Isaiah's word alone proves a virginal conception; his narrative reports that conception and then reads Isaiah's sign as answering to it. Luke's independent account (Luke 1:26-38) tells the same conception without citing Isaiah, though Gabriel's words to Mary echo the birth formula of 7:14.

verses.context: The sign comes with a clock. Before the child is old enough to know right from wrong, a matter of a few years, the lands of the two kings Ahaz fears will be deserted. The child will eat curds and honey, a detail verse 22 will explain in a darker key.
verses.grammar: Ledato, "By the time He knows", is an infinitive construct with the preposition le, which can mean ‘at the time of his knowing’ or ‘so that he may know’; most translators take it as temporal. Maos bara uvachor battov, ‘to reject the evil and choose the good’, uses two infinitives absolute and describes the age of moral discernment, as in Deuteronomy 1:39, where the little ones who do not yet know good from evil are spared. Chemah udevash, "curds and honey", can be a sign of plenty (a land flowing with milk and honey) or of poverty, the food of herders in a land whose fields have gone wild. Verses 21 and 22 show that Isaiah means the second: the diet of survivors in a depopulated land.
verses.history: The timetable was met. Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC, executed Rezin, and deported its people (2 Kings 16:9); in the same campaigns he annexed Galilee and Gilead and left Israel a rump state around Samaria (2 Kings 15:29). Within about two or three years of the prophecy, the lands of both kings had been laid waste.

verses.context: The other edge of the sign. The same child's lifetime will see the worst days since the kingdom split, and the cause will be the power Ahaz is courting: the king of Assyria. The verse transitions from the personal oracle to the four ‘on that day’ oracles that follow.
verses.grammar: Yavi YHWH, "The LORD will bring", is a Hiphil imperfect: God is the one who brings Assyria, not Ahaz. The phrase "since the day Ephraim separated from Judah" uses sur, ‘to turn aside, depart’, for the schism. The last words, et melekh Ashur, "the king of Assyria", stand awkwardly at the end of the sentence, and a number of critical commentators regard them as an explanatory addition; if so, the addition simply names what the chapter already implies.
verses.history: The division of the kingdom came after Solomon's death, around 930 BC, when the northern tribes rejected Rehoboam (1 Kings 12). Assyria's coming would bring worse: Samaria fell in 722 BC, and in 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah. His annals, preserved on clay prisms, claim that he took forty-six of Hezekiah's fortified cities and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.

theology.note: The ally Ahaz chose becomes the instrument of his judgment. Isaiah 10:5 will call Assyria the rod of God's anger; the chapter shows judgment arriving through the very choices that refused trust.

verses.context: The first of four ‘on that day’ oracles. The LORD whistles, and the two great powers come like insects: flies from Egypt, bees from Assyria. They settle everywhere, in ravines, rock clefts, thornbushes, and watering places, so no corner of the land is untouched.
verses.grammar: Yishroq, "will whistle", is the verb Isaiah used in 5:26 for God whistling up a distant nation, as a beekeeper might call bees. "The farthest streams of the Nile" translates biqtseh yeorei Mitsrayim, ‘the end of the channels of Egypt’: yeor, an Egyptian loanword for the Nile, in the plural means its branches and canals, the delta where flies swarm. The four places in verse 19 move from wild terrain to cultivated resources, a complete inventory of the land.

theology.note: Egypt and Assyria were the superpowers of Isaiah's world, and Judah's politics swung between them. Isaiah pictures both as insects that come when God whistles. The oracle does not deny their power; it places it under his.

verses.context: The second oracle is a single sharp image. The Lord will shave Judah with a hired razor from beyond the Euphrates, the king of Assyria, taking head, body hair, and beard. The picture is humiliation, not merely defeat.
verses.grammar: Betaar hasekhirah, "a razor hired", is the point of the verse: sakhir means hired, and Ahaz had just hired Assyria with temple silver (2 Kings 16:8). The Lord now uses the same hired blade against the hirer. "Beyond the Euphrates" is beevrei nahar, ‘beyond the River’, the standard way of naming Mesopotamia from Israel. "The hair of your legs" is literally ‘the hair of the feet’, where raglayim is probably a euphemism for the private parts, as it seems to be elsewhere (Isaiah 6:2 is debated), so the shaving strips the whole body.
verses.history: Shaving a man's beard against his will was a grave insult in the ancient Near East: when the Ammonite king Hanun shaved half the beards of David's envoys, it was an act of war (2 Samuel 10:4-6). Deportees and captives were also sometimes shaved. The image tells Judah that Assyria will treat it as a conquered, shamed people.

verses.context: The third oracle describes life after the invasion. A man keeps one heifer and two sheep, and there is so little population that the milk is abundant, so everyone left eats curds and honey. The food of verse 15 is now explained: plenty for the few, because the many are gone.
verses.grammar: Yechayyeh, "will raise", is a Piel of chayah, ‘to keep alive’: the farmer is keeping a remnant of livestock alive, not building a herd. "All who remain" is kol-hannotar, a Niphal participle of yatar, ‘to be left over’, the language of the remnant that runs through Isaiah (1:9, 4:3). The abundance is ironic: milk overflows only because there are so few mouths.

theology.note: The remnant survives but in a land emptied of people and fields. Isaiah's theme of the remnant (named already in Shear-jashub, verse 3) includes both mercy and loss: some are kept, many are not.

verses.context: The last oracle reverses the land's value. Prime vineyards worth a silver shekel a vine become thickets of briers and thorns, hunting ground for archers, and the terraced hills once worked by hoe become pasture for cattle and sheep. The chapter that began with a king worried about a siege ends with the countryside gone wild.
verses.grammar: The pair shamir vashayit, "briers and thorns", repeated three times in these verses, is Isaiah's signature phrase for judgment on the land (5:6, 9:18, 10:17, 27:4). It ties this oracle to the Song of the Vineyard in 5:1-7, where God's vineyard, Israel, is left to the same thorns. "A thousand vines worth a thousand shekels" (elef gefen beelef kasef) prices a vineyard at a shekel per vine. Yeaderun, ‘they used to be hoed’, is a Niphal imperfect describing a past habit, the careful handwork of terraced hillside farming.

theology.note: The land's fruitfulness is bound up with the people's faithfulness, the pattern of Deuteronomy 28 and of Isaiah's vineyard song. The thorns recall the curse on the ground in Genesis 3:18, and Isaiah's later promises reverse them: instead of the thornbush, the cypress (Isaiah 55:13).
